prompt: Linda is described as outspoken, a philosophy graduate concerned with social justice. Most people judge “Linda is a bank teller and a feminist” more likely than “Linda is a bank teller”. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: This is the conjunction fallacy
It is driven by the representativeness heuristic
P(bank teller AND feminist) can never be higher than P(bank teller)
The answer is correct if Linda is very likely to be a feminist

explanation: However likely “feminist” is, the conjunction is a subset of “bank teller”: P(A∩B) ≤ P(A). With 5 % and 95 % (independent) the conjunction is 4.75 % < 5 %.

prompt: A study finds that firms with a Chief Sustainability Officer have higher profits. Which explanations would be sources of endogeneity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Profitable firms can afford to hire a CSO (reverse causation)
Firm size drives both having a CSO and profitability (omitted variable)
Only surviving firms are in the database (selection / survivorship bias)
The sample includes both firms with and without a CSO

explanation: Reverse causation, omitted (confounding) variables, measurement error and selection bias are the four sources of endogeneity. Comparing firms with and without a CSO is necessary, but does not by itself create endogeneity.

prompt: An experienced airline executive applies the hub-and-spoke model he knows to a new low-cost subsidiary, ignoring point-to-point alternatives. Which concept describes this best?

options.text: Einstellung effect (cognitive entrenchment)
Out-group homogeneity bias
Conjunction fallacy
Inattentional blindness

explanation: Expertise creates stable schemas; the Einstellung effect is prioritizing the known solution over new and potentially more appropriate ones (Dane 2010).

prompt: Which are the three mechanisms of confirmation bias presented in class?

options.text: Selective exposure, selective perception, selective retention
Anchoring, framing, priming
Simultaneity, omitted variable, measurement error
Awareness, motivation, ability

explanation: We expose ourselves to, evaluate positively and remember information that fits our prior beliefs. Personalized internet search and social media amplify this (filter bubble).

prompt: During WWII, analysts proposed armouring the parts of returning bombers that showed the most bullet holes. Abraham Wald disagreed. Why?

options.text: Planes hit in other places did not return, so the undamaged areas of returning planes were the critical ones
Bullet holes were measured with error
Returning planes were a random sample of all planes
Armour has no effect on survival

explanation: Survivorship bias: only survivors were observed. The areas without holes on survivors are those where hits were fatal – these should be reinforced.

prompt: According to Kahneman, Lovallo & Sibony (2011), what is the most effective way to limit biases in strategic decisions?

options.text: Have an independent reviewer check the recommending team's proposal with a checklist
Train each executive to recognize his or her own biases
Let the CEO state a clear preference early so the team can focus
Rely on the intuition of the most experienced manager

explanation: We cannot catch our own intuitive errors, but we can apply System 2 to others' recommendations. The reviewer must be independent; a leader who signals a preference early becomes part of the team (and triggers self-censorship).

prompt: Which correctives do Sunstein & Hastie (2014) recommend to make groups smarter? Select all that apply.

options.text: Silence the leader at the start of the discussion
Establish a contrarian (red) team
Use anonymous estimates (Delphi method)
Reward each member for being individually right rather than for the group outcome

explanation: They recommend rewarding group success (not individual calls), assigning roles, priming critical thinking, red teams and Delphi. A formally appointed devil's advocate helps less than authentic dissent.

prompt: Which statement about the two thinking systems is correct according to the course?

options.text: Both System 1 and System 2 processes can be correct or biased
Biases come only from System 1, System 2 is always normatively correct
System 2 is fast and associative
The two systems never operate at the same time

explanation: The slides call it a fallacy to assume System 1 is responsible for biases and System 2 for correct answers. The systems operate in parallel (“switching cognitive gears”).

prompt: A survey on employee satisfaction is answered mainly by employees who like the company; dissatisfied employees ignore it. Which bias is this?

options.text: Non-response bias (a form of selection bias)
Measurement error
Reverse causation
Conjunction fallacy

explanation: People who refuse to participate differ systematically from those who take part – a selection bias. Related: volunteer, attrition, undercoverage, survivorship bias.

statement: Bounded rationality means that decision-makers evaluate all alternatives but sometimes make calculation mistakes.
explanation: Simon: decision-makers do not evaluate all alternatives; they pick the first satisfactory one (satisficing), using heuristics to save mental effort.

statement: Heuristics usually work, but they are not always accurate.
explanation: They are mental shortcuts between automatic perception and deliberate reasoning (Kahneman 2002).

statement: In-group favoritism only appears when group members share a long history.
explanation: Experiments show in-group favoritism even when individuals are randomly assigned to groups (social identity theory).

statement: Out-group homogeneity bias means we perceive members of other groups as more similar to each other than members of our own group.
explanation: “They are alike; we are diverse.” Out-group members are perceived as close to the typical member.

statement: A spurious correlation between A and B can be produced by a third variable that affects both.
explanation: Omitted variable / confounding variable bias – e.g. hot weather drives both ice-cream consumption and sunburn.

statement: Temporal antecedence helps against reverse causation: if A happens before B, B cannot be a cause of A.
explanation: Other remedies: theory, controlled experiments, instrumental variables.

statement: According to Kahneman et al. (2011), being aware of cognitive biases is enough to avoid them.
explanation: Awareness does almost nothing; System 1 errors are invisible to ourselves. The remedy is reviewing others' proposals and designing the decision process.

statement: Deliberation in groups tends to make members' views more moderate.
explanation: Group polarization: deliberation pushes groups towards a more extreme version of their initial leaning (Sunstein & Hastie).

statement: Cognitive load, such as multitasking, increases the probability of inattentional blindness.
explanation: Other causes: an unremarkable object, expectations, limited attentional capacities.

statement: Powell, Lovallo & Fox (2011) argue that firm-level choice architecture is more promising than trying to debias individual managers.
explanation: Biases are embedded in routines, norms and politics. Example: a pharma firm created a separate divestment team to counter escalation of commitment.

prompt: Explain the four sources of endogeneity using the question “Does a larger marketing budget increase a firm's sales?”.
modelAnswer: Reverse causation: firms with higher sales may get larger budgets (budgets are often set as % of sales). Omitted variable: a confounder such as firm size or a booming market raises both budget and sales, creating a spurious correlation. Measurement error: “marketing budget” or “sales” may be badly measured (which spending counts, which period, which markets?). Selection bias: the sample may contain only surviving or listed firms, or only firms that chose to report – so the relation is not representative. To claim causality: theory, temporal ordering, controlled or natural experiments (e.g. randomly switching off ads in some regions, as eBay did).
keyPoints: Reverse causation applied to the example

prompt: A CEO wants to copy the strategy of a famous unicorn because “all successful platforms grew fast before making profits”. Identify two biases in this reasoning and propose how the board should review the decision.
modelAnswer: Survivorship bias: the CEO only looks at successful platforms; many that also grew fast before profits failed and are invisible, so fast growth may not cause success. Saliency/halo effect: one memorable success story is used as the analogy and its reputation is taken as evidence. Possible further biases: confirmation bias, over-optimism. Review: an independent reviewer applies the Kahneman checklist – ask for several comparable cases including failures (reference-class forecasting), check where the numbers come from (anchoring), run a premortem (“imagine the strategy failed in three years – why?”), and set up a red team arguing against the plan.
keyPoints: Second bias (halo, saliency, confirmation, over-optimism) explained
Concrete tools: reference class incl. failures, premortem, red team

prompt: Why is categorization both useful and dangerous for strategic decision-makers?
modelAnswer: Useful: putting things into categories with prototypes lets us respond quickly; diagnosing a problem is itself an act of categorization, and mapping an industry requires understanding categorical boundaries. Dangerous: categories bring prototypes that think for us – representativeness (conjunction fallacy), out-group homogeneity, in-group favoritism and dichotomous (black-and-white) thinking. A decision is a binary go/no-go, but strategic problems are ambiguous, so black-and-white reasoning can misidentify and mis-solve the problem. Expertise helps to see real similarities, but can lead to entrenchment (Einstellung). Remedy: check the assumptions behind each similarity judgement.
keyPoints: Speed / diagnosis as categorization / industry mapping
